justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modestly bullish near-term outlook for the underlying asset, likely an equity index or ETF trading around the 570 level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts that would cause a large directional move. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects the historical tendency of equity markets to trend modestly higher over short-to-medium horizons when no clear bearish catalyst is present, combined with any prevailing momentum signal at the time of the forecast. The incremental step-up from 570 to 572.5 to 578 is deliberately conservative, acknowledging that drift over weeks is real but modest relative to volatility.

Confidence interval widths were calibrated to grow with the time horizon in a way consistent with a square-root-of-time scaling of volatility. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 13.5 points corresponds to an implied daily volatility of around 1.2%, which is consistent with typical realized volatility for a large-cap index ETF. By one week, the interval widens to approximately plus or minus 24.5 points, and by one month it expands to roughly plus or minus 48 points. These widths incorporate not just statistical volatility but also the possibility of regime shifts, earnings surprises, or macroeconomic data releases that could alter the prevailing trend during the forecast window.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include an unexpected Federal Reserve policy announcement or shift in forward guidance, a significant geopolitical event, a major corporate earnings miss from a large index constituent, or a sudden liquidity event in credit markets that triggers equity risk-off selling. On the upside, a better-than-expected inflation print, a surprise trade deal, or a dovish pivot could generate a rally that breaches the upper bound. The one-month interval is the most vulnerable to tail events simply because more time elapses for such surprises to materialize.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume relatively stable market conditions and do not fully account for fat-tailed distributions inherent in equity returns. In practice, the true probability of an outcome outside a 90% confidence interval constructed from normal assumptions is somewhat higher than 10%, particularly at the monthly horizon. Black swan events, by definition, are underrepresented in historical data and therefore in any model that relies on it.
